title: The bent woman (Luke 13:10–17)
hook: eighteen years bent over, healed on the sabbath, and she stands straight

segments.voice: Yesterday, a gardener begged one more year for a fig tree with no figs. Your line was let it alone this year. Who did you give more time? Day four hundred sixty-six.

Try this for a moment, wherever you are. Let your head drop and your back curl until you're looking at the floor. Stay there. You can see feet, and dust, and the hem of other people's clothes. You can't see a face unless someone bends down to you. Now imagine that for eighteen years. Going to the market like that. Going to synagogue like that, every sabbath, for eighteen years. Luke says there was a woman who lived exactly this way, and one sabbath Jesus was teaching in her synagogue. Today, the bent woman.
screen: `LOOK AT THE FLOOR. STAY THERE.` → `EIGHTEEN YEARS OF FEET AND DUST.` → `ONE SABBATH IN THE SYNAGOGUE.`

segments.voice: Luke describes her carefully: "there was a woman who had a spirit of infirmity eighteen years: and she was bent down, neither could she look upwards at all." Notice she doesn't ask for anything. She's simply there, in her usual place, doing what she always did: showing up to pray. Jesus sees her and calls her over. He says: "Woman, thou art delivered from thy infirmity." He lays his hands on her, and immediately she's made straight, and she glorifies God. Picture it: the first face she sees from upright in eighteen years. Then a complication. The ruler of the synagogue is indignant, because it's the sabbath, and he tells the crowd: there are six days for work. Come and be healed on those, not on the sabbath. It's worth being fair to him. Keeping the sabbath holy was, and is, a deep act of faithfulness for Jews, and he's trying to protect it. Jesus answers from inside that same faithfulness. Every one of you, he says, unties his ox or his donkey on the sabbath and leads it to water. And this woman, a daughter of Abraham, whom Satan has bound these eighteen years, shouldn't she be untied on the sabbath day? Daughter of Abraham. It's a phrase almost nobody uses in the Gospels, and it gives her back her full place in God's people. The sabbath, in Jesus' reading, is exactly the day for setting someone free. Luke ends with the crowd rejoicing at all the glorious things he was doing. Eighteen years of looking at the floor, and then she stood up.
screen: `EIGHTEEN YEARS, BENT DOWN.` · `WOMAN, THOU ART DELIVERED.` · `THE OX UNTIED ON THE SABBATH.` · `A DAUGHTER OF ABRAHAM.` · then, large: `SHE WAS MADE STRAIGHT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: stand up straight and give thanks. If you're able, stand. If not, sit tall. Start bent: let your head drop and your shoulders curl. Breathe there a moment. Then, slowly, unroll your spine one piece at a time, until your head rises and you're looking straight ahead. Feel your chest open. Breathe into it. Think of one thing you're grateful for today. If you pray, give thanks to God the way she did. If you don't, simply let yourself feel glad to be upright. The bell holds the time.
The bent woman. Eighteen years unable to look up, healed by Jesus on the sabbath and called a daughter of Abraham. Today's word.
Your line: she stood up. Today, every time you notice yourself hunched over a screen, stand up straight, look up, and say thanks. Day four hundred sixty-six.

howItsDone: Catholics pray for the sick at Mass and through the sacrament of the Anointing of the Sick, in which the priest lays hands on the sick person, as Jesus did here.

fork.setup: you lead the synagogue. a teacher has just healed a woman on the sabbath, and the crowd is buzzing. what do you say?
options: there are six days for healing. come on those.
praise God, and invite him to teach again.
fork.reveal: he says come on the other six days. Jesus answers: you untie your ox on the sabbath, so why not a daughter of Abraham?

trapdoor: what you thought: this story is about Jesus breaking a rule.
what it means: Jesus argues from within sabbath faithfulness that the sabbath is the right day to set a daughter of Abraham free.
what a scholar hears: the verb for her being made straight (anorthoo) is used in the Greek Psalms of God raising up those bowed down; daughter of Abraham is very rare.

sources.quoted: there was a woman who had a spirit of infirmity eighteen years: and she was bent down, neither could she look upwards at all.

notes: Confirm Douay-Rheims wording of Luke 13:11 and 13:12.

Trapdoor: anorthoo appears in the Septuagint Psalm 145(146):8 ('the Lord lifts up those bowed down'); confirm. 'Daughter of Abraham' occurs only here in the New Testament; the voice says 'almost nobody uses' to be safe.
Fair framing of the synagogue ruler and sabbath observance: confirm acceptable to both Catholic and Jewish readers.
The practice asks listeners to curl and uncurl the spine; offered with a seated alternative for those with limited mobility.
